summary: After two iterations, our best approach (simulated annealing with greedy initialization) scores 84-86 on the judge. The iter-2 hypothesis that multi-restart SA would outperform single-run SA was refuted — the mean difference was only +0.19 points (84.53 vs 84.34), well within ±2 point judge variance. The SA inner loop and move set from iter-1 remain the dominant performance driver.
key_points: Iteration 1 established that simple SA moves with high iteration throughput beat complex compound moves (score ~84.5). Spatial indexing, weighted selection, and boundary-swap moves all hurt by reducing iterations per second.

Iteration 2 tested multi-restart SA (3 restarts with shuffled greedy ordering) vs single-run SA. Result: mean 84.53 vs 84.34 — no statistically meaningful difference given ±2 point judge variance. Hypothesis refuted.

Dead ends confirmed: BSP initialization (72.5), sorted greedy (83.6), weighted rectangle selection (83.6), 5 restarts (86.0 but inconsistent), and temperature tuning (marginal). The current 8-move uniform SA with linear cooling is a strong local optimum for this approach.

Key unknowns: (1) Can a fundamentally different move — e.g., simultaneously shifting a shared boundary between adjacent rectangles — improve SA quality without hurting throughput? (2) Would a two-phase approach (coarse placement via assignment/LP, then SA refinement) break out of the 84-86 plateau? (3) Is there a better cooling schedule (e.g., reheating) that could help?

Recommended next iteration: Focus on a well-implemented 'boundary shift' move that identifies adjacent rectangles sharing an edge and moves that edge, adjusting both rectangles atomically. This is the most promising unexplored direction — it directly addresses the core constraint (non-overlapping rectangles with target areas) without the throughput penalty of the failed v3 attempt. Alternatively, try adaptive move selection that biases toward whichever move type is currently producing accepted improvements.
